item.title: Ubuntu on WSL finally replaced my Linux partition, and my Windows 11 PC no longer needs dual-boot
item.itunes:title: Ubuntu on WSL finally replaced my Linux partition, and my Windows 11 PC no longer needs dual-boot
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My first encounter with the Windows Subsystem for Linux was when I had to install it to run Docker containers for uni projects. For the longest time, WSL was merely the backend engine for my Windows-powered containerization experiments, while a dedicated Ubuntu partition was responsible for housing typical Linux apps.

But over time, I realized such a setup had plenty of caveats, and began tinkering with virtual machines. Sadly, VM-only projects had a major drawback in the form of extra performance overheads, and that’s when I finally turned my attention to WSL. Although it took me a few days to get accustomed to WSL’s quirks and commands, it single-handedly replaced my dual-boot partition for my Linux workloads.

I tested dual-boot, WSL2, and VMs to run Linux apps on Windows, and only one was worth keeping

Dual-boot, VMs, and WSL2 walk into a Windows PC...

10
By  Ayush Pande

Maintaining dual-boot environments on the same SSD is really annoying

And I’d rather not buy yet another drive for Linux with current SSD prices

On the surface, setting up Linux and Windows boot partitions on the same drive doesn’t take a lot of effort. For my setup, I installed Windows 11 first, and then went down the Linux rabbit hole with good ol’ Ubuntu. This configuration worked pretty well for a few weeks, until a major Windows 11 update overwrote the GRUB bootloader and rendered my Linux installation unusable, and I had to rely on a live USB to repair it.

An easy way to circumvent this problem would be switching to a different SSD, which isn’t as easy as it used to be a few years ago. After all, the prices of SSDs have gotten extremely out of hand as of late. If I wanted a second drive specifically for my Linux shenanigans, I’d be shelling out well over $150 just to get a decent 1TB SSD for an Ubuntu installation. And since I already have a 2TB primary drive that I bought aeons ago, letting it run a handful of Windows apps and grabbing a new SSD just for Linux isn’t very economical.

Another minor gripe I have with dual-boot setups is that I’d have to switch between operating systems a handful of times during projects. It’s not a deal-breaker by any means, but having to reboot my PC, change the bootloader, and log into another OS just to run a single application can get a little tedious.

I ditched my Debian VM for the immutable Lightwhale OS, and Docker containers have never been simpler

Docker host that runs itself.

5
By  Samir Makwana

WSL lets me use Windows and Ubuntu seamlessly

It’s also more responsive than typical VMs

Switching to WSL got rid of the problems I’d faced with my dual-boot setup. For one, running Ubuntu (or any other Linux distro) on top of Windows 11 means I don’t need to deal with the problems of a shared SSD or allocate an entire boot drive to a Linux flavor. Plus, if I want to switch to my Windows 11 e-sports titles, I can just close the WSL window, and the same holds true about swapping back to my Linux escapades.

Technically, running virtual machines via VirtualBox, VMware Workstation Pro, or even good ol’ Hyper-V would net the same results. But I’d have to contend with the extra resources drained by such a setup. After all, running a full-on virtual machine siphons a lot more resources than WSL2, even if said VM has a minimal CLI OS. I’d also have to look into shared clipboard settings, install an OS, and tinker with the finer management aspects of the VM before I can get any meaningful work done.

Of course, running a CLI distro bare-metal will have even less overhead than WSL2. But for everything from regular coding work and Linux terminal misadventures to DevOps projects and even GUI apps, WSL2 delivers a responsive experience. That’s something I’ve started to prioritize ever since the rising PC hardware prices stopped me from upgrading my old daily driver. Not to mention, sharing files between my WSL instances and Windows is extremely straightforward, and setting up a fresh distro on WSL takes a lot less than it does in a typical VM.

Even GUI apps mesh well with WSL

And the same goes for services that support GPU acceleration

Over the years, I've started relying more on CLI apps and services featuring web UIs for my Linux projects. But when push comes to shove and I need to access FOSS Linux utilities that are designed around, I can simply launch them from WSL, and they work fine without needing any tweaks whatsoever.

The same holds true for GPU accelerated tasks, which is something I can’t even imagine on typical virtual machines. As long as I’ve got the CUDA toolkit up and running within my WSL distros, I can use my RTX 3080 Ti for my LLM training workloads, CAD tools, and even random Python environments.

WSL is the sole reason I use Windows 11 on my daily driver

Since my everyday tasks involve a healthy mixture of Linux and Windows, I can’t ditch either OS family. Thanks to WSL, I can experiment with Linux projects at near-native performance, tinker with Ubuntu’s filesystem, and run GPU-accelerated tasks directly on top of my Windows 11 setup.

Windows Subsystem for Linux
See at Github

item.title: These VS Code settings solved my code review headaches before they even started
item.itunes:title: These VS Code settings solved my code review headaches before they even started
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I love using VS Code. It's my favorite integrated development environment (IDE) and my top Microsoft software pick. Obsidian is great, but it's no IDE replacement, at least not for me. That said, VS Code still needs a few tweaks to make it even better. I rounded up a few setting adjustments I always make before writing a single line of code in a new project. Some may alter the way you work while others are simply cosmetic.

Format on save

This is a must-have

This one configuration allows VS Code to perform an automatic cleanup pass with each save, and it's one of the first I add to a new project. Instead of wasting time in YAML or any other type of file perfecting indentation, spacing, quotes, and line breaks while coding, VS Code can handle this work for you. It's brilliant.

"editor.formatOnSave": true

It's not perfect, however, and checks will need to be made to ensure VS Code is using a complete and consistent formatting configuration; otherwise, you'll end up with some weird results. When writing and editing code, I prefer to remain firmly in the zone when it comes to structure and behavior. I don't want to think about correct placement, which is precisely what this single setting addresses.

I finally found the perfect code editor after years of switching back and forth

My coding workflow found its home.

11
By  Parth Shah

Getting rid of whitespace

Trailing in the rear and causing trouble

Trailing whitespace is like that group of kids from school that would always sit at the rear of the coach and cause a racket, throwing paper balls at everyone in front. It's just as annoying and can result in Git diffs being recorded, code review comments, and weird Markdown behavior. It can also be a pain for web applications such as MediaWiki.

"files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true

This setting ensures VS Code removes it whenever files are saved. It's worth noting that this can remove whitespace that is actually manually entered into a file, so if you did want that line break, it would need to be re-added post-saving. But it's well worth having, since depending on what you're working on and where the whitespace is, making legitimate changes can be harder to review.

Append a new line at file end

Great for keeping Git healthy and happy

Did you know that not having a new line at the end of a file could lead to Git pointing out the fact? Many Unix tools and conventions expect files to end with a new line, which is precisely what this VS Code setting achieves. It simply appends a new line at the end of the file. It's wonderful, automatic, and can save a few headaches.

"files.insertFinalNewline": true

It's a similar theme to the rest of my setting alteration recommendations in that they all come together to solve tiny inconsistencies before reaching source control. I don't want to see any code-review comments asking for a new line to be added to the bottom of a file and I'm sure you don't either. This addresses that.

4 VS Code forks built for specific tasks

The classic VS Code is great and all, but these specialized forks are better for certain programming tasks

By  Ayush Pande

Smooth cursor operator

Everything looks so smooooooth

Are you coding late at night or simply wishing for your cursor blinker to stop blinking so blinking quickly? That's precisely where cursorBlinking comes into play. Setting it to smooth slows down the animation and makes the entire interface a more relaxing view to gaze at for hours at a time. It may do absolutely nothing for you, but I'm a big fan of this.

"editor.cursorBlinking": "smooth" 
"editor.cursorSmoothCaretAnimation": "on"

Similarly, cursorSmoothCaretAnimation being enabled shows that not every preference alteration will save hours of development work. Some will simply alter the appearance and experience of using VS Code for longer periods. With these two settings configured as such, you'll have a smooth cursor gliding across the interface.

Configure project language defaults

One size does not fit all

What may work for me in PHP, HTML, or even some CSS won't likely do the job as well for your C project. That's where project language defaults come in to save the day. This allows you to configure each setting accordingly, depending on which language is used. For instance, I may want formatOnSave set to true for both TypeScript and Python, but only have rulers enabled in the latter language profile.

"[typescript]": { 
 "editor.defaultFormatter": "esbenp.prettier-vscode", 
 "editor.formatOnSave": true 
}, 
"[python]": { 
 "editor.formatOnSave": true, 
 "editor.rulers": [88] 
}

Using the above, this is not only possible but highly encouraged if you find yourself working with different languages. Personal and ergonomic settings can be applied on a global scale, whereas language-specific adjustments can be made on a project or workspace basis. It's a testament to how customizable VS Code is, allowing one to personalize it with language-specific alterations to be as productive as possible.

7 reasons VS Code is the best text editor, even if you're not a developer

The secret text editor everyone should be using

3
By  Parth Shah

Making the most of your IDE

It's vital you don't settle for the default experience offered by IDEs. They're there to help make your life easier, so it's only right you spend the invaluable couple of minutes looking up some settings, plugins, and guides in order to make the most of the available features and functionality. The more tuned the setup is to your requirements and project, the more you'll get done in the same allotted time. I've saved valuable seconds with each session, better spent with loved ones and then some.

I've had a Sony STR-DH520 driving the same pile of speakers since 2011, and every time I test a new soundbar, I land on the same conclusion. It's not even close, and you can buy a used AV receiver for the price of a cheap soundbar to hear it for yourself. A real center channel, real surrounds, and a subwoofer I can park wherever the room likes. It beats beamforming tricks and up-firing drivers.

But something has been quietly going wrong with that setup, and it isn't the amplifier. Put a modern TV in the middle of it, and suddenly Netflix sounds like stereo, DTS vanishes, and your console insists it's outputting 2.0. The easy answer is to blame eARC, plug everything into your TV's eARC port, and move on. That's part of it, but the real problem starts a step earlier.

Modern TVs have made themselves the center of your home theater

And ARC was never built to carry that much

Fifteen years ago, the receiver was the hub. The Blu-ray player, console, and cable box all plugged in; it decoded the audio, and it passed the video along to the TV. That still works, right up until you want 4K. Receivers from that era have HDMI 1.4 ports and an old version of HDCP, the copy protection every device in the chain has to support, so they can't pass protected 4K content at all. HDR, 4K at 120Hz, and VRR are out too, so if your console runs through an old receiver, your PS5 is probably plugged into the wrong HDMI port.

So you do what everyone does. The sources go into the TV, and the audio comes back to the receiver over HDMI ARC. Sound & Vision recommends that exact workaround, and it's where the compromises begin.

ARC

eARC

Introduced

HDMI 1.4 (2009)

HDMI 2.1 (2017)

Multichannel PCM

No, stereo only

Up to 8 channels, 24-bit/192kHz

Dolby TrueHD, DTS-HD MA

No

Yes

Dolby Digital, DTS, DD+

Yes (lossy)

Yes

ARC can carry two-channel PCM, compressed Dolby Digital and DTS at 5.1, and Dolby Digital Plus on TVs that support it, but nothing lossless. eARC fixes that, but both ends need to support it, and a 2011 receiver doesn't. My STR-DH520 at least has plain ARC. Some receivers from that era don't, which leaves you on optical, a 40-year-old AV standard that's killing your surround sound with the same lossy ceiling and no CEC.

The kicker is that the STR-DH520 already decodes Dolby TrueHD and DTS-HD Master Audio over its four HDMI inputs. It was a $229 receiver in 2011, and it can handle lossless formats just fine. The formats aren't the problem. The return path is.

Your TV is quietly deciding what your receiver gets to hear

It's not only an eARC problem

If ARC's bandwidth were the whole story, you'd at least get a solid lossy 5.1 out of everything. You often don't, because the TV sits in the middle and decides what to pass along. DTS is the obvious casualty. LG dropped DTS in 2020, brought it back in 2023, and removed it again from 2025 models like the C5 and G5, whose EDID no longer lists DTS. Samsung owners have been complaining about the lack of DTS since the 2018 Q9FN. If the TV doesn't accept DTS, your player falls back to something else, and your receiver never sees a track it could have decoded just fine.

Dolby Digital Plus is sneakier. My STR-DH520 happens to decode it, but most receivers sold before 2012 can't. When a streaming track has a standard Dolby Digital core, the TV can pass it through as 5.1. When it doesn't — which is increasingly common with Atmos streams — the TV decodes it and downmixes it to stereo PCM. That's the likeliest reason your favorite show suddenly sounds flat.

Consoles have their own quirks. A PS5 set to Linear PCM gives you stereo over ARC. Switch it to Dolby Audio, and you get real 5.1, but compressed to around 640 kbps. An Xbox can encode Dolby Digital or DTS on the fly for ARC, which is better, but it's still lossy.

And then there's the setting where almost nobody checks. If the TV's digital audio output is set to PCM, it downmixes everything to two channels, regardless of what the source sends. Some TVs also pass 5.1 from their built-in apps but only stereo from external HDMI inputs, which can feel random. It isn't random. It's the TV.

The Nvidia Shield TV isn't fast anymore, so I tried to find out why nobody has actually replaced it

It's about more than just speed.

27
By  Anurag Singh

You don't need a soundbar to fix this; you need a small box

The receiver was never the weak link

Soundbar makers love this situation, because their answer is eARC in one box with one cable. To be fair, that's a real advantage. A modern soundbar decodes Atmos, handles CEC volume control, and pulls lossless audio out of the TV without any fuss. My STR-DH520 can't do Atmos; it has no room correction, and no adapter changes either. But it still pushes 100W into each of seven channels, with a proper center channel, real surrounds, and a separate subwoofer, and a soundbar has to fake at least one of those.

The fix is to grab the audio before the TV mangles it. An eARC audio extractor connects to the TV's eARC port and hands the audio to one of the receiver's regular HDMI inputs, so the receiver treats it like any other source. The OREI BK-927 is $80 on sale and passes 7.1 PCM, TrueHD, and DTS-HD MA untouched. The HDFury Arcana 2 costs $349, but its COPY output feeds older receivers a downscaled 1080p stream with full audio and adds CEC volume control.

If you'd rather not buy anything, set the TV's output to passthrough or bitstream, set your console to Dolby or DTS, and accept lossy 5.1. It's the same compromise as optical, but it beats stereo by a mile. You can also plug a Blu-ray player directly into the receiver and enjoy 1080p for movie night.

Your soundbar's HDMI port is lying to you, and PC gamers need to know why

HDMI ARC isn't what you think it is

2
By  Samarveer Singh

Your old amplifier is still good, but the connectivity standards changed

The amplifier didn't age out. HDMI did, and TVs took full advantage. If your receiver still sounds great, don't let a TV's audio menu talk you into a soundbar. Check that output setting, spend $80 on an extractor, and keep the speakers you already love.

item.title: Qualcomm isn't ruling out Snapdragon X2-powered gaming handhelds
item.itunes:title: Qualcomm isn't ruling out Snapdragon X2-powered gaming handhelds
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Qualcomm has hinted that X-series chips could appear in dedicated gaming handhelds.
  • Some existing handhelds use Snapdragon G mobile-focused chips, but not the X or X2 series.
  • Notable hurdles include Windows game compatibility via Microsoft's Prism emulation and anti‑cheat issues in multiplayer titles.

On paper, Qualcomm's Arm-based Snapdragon X2 series chips seem like a solid fit for a high-end dedicated gaming handheld, given their strong CPU/GPU performance and battery-life efficiency. So far, though, we've only seen Snapdragon G-Series chips in Android-focused handhelds from companies like Retroid, OneXPlayer, and Ayaneo.

However, that could change in the future. During a roundtable interview at the Snapdragon Summit, I asked Kedar Kondap, Qualcomm's GM of Compute and Gaming, if there's a possibility we'll eventually see Snapdragon X series chips, like the Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme, X2 Plus, or X2 Elite, in an ROG Xbox Ally X-like Windows 11 gaming handheld at some point.

While Kondap didn't outright say this is something that's actually happening, he emphasized that "the interest is pretty high in terms of gaming devices," hinting that it's something we might see in the future and stating that, from a technical perspective, nothing is preventing a manufacturer from featuring, for example, the 18-core X2 Elite Extreme in a dedicated gaming handheld.

"...the good part for us now is that we support various operating systems. It provides the benefit, right? So, for example, today we have multiple handhelds, but not with the X series; we have them with our mobile platforms and our gaming-specific platforms," said Kondap.

Several gaming handhelds already feature Qualcomm chips, but not the X2 series

Game compatibility would likely be at least somewhat of an issue

Kondap then mentioned the Snapdragon 680 featured in the streaming-focused PlayStation Portal and the Snapdragon 720G in the Lenovo Legion Play. "There are [gaming] devices already [that feature Qualcomm chips]. They range from streaming-only devices to devices that can run native games, to handhelds purpose-built for gaming. The first two we already have in market," said Kondap.

From a graphics performance perspective, the Adreno X2-90 GPU in the Arm64 Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme is somewhat comparable to Intel's impressive Panther Lake-based Arc B390 integrated graphics, which is featured in the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+.

Other hurdles remain, including the fact that many x86/x64 Windows games would need to run through Microsoft's Prism translation layer on an Arm64 Snapdragon X2 handheld. That's an additional compatibility barrier the x86-based Steam Deck doesn't face when running Windows games through Proton, or something AMD-powered handhelds like the ROG Xbox Ally X have to deal with.

There's also the issue of anti-cheat compatibility, which currently prevents several major multiplayer games, including Valorant, Sea of Thieves, and Rocket League, from running on Windows on Arm.

Qualcomm split its 2026 flagship Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chip into two tiers, and both hit 5GHz

Unsurprisingly, the chip giant is going even more all-in on AI.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: I started editing my videos with this free open-source CapCut alternative, and my workflow got faster
item.itunes:title: I started editing my videos with this free open-source CapCut alternative, and my workflow got faster
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Free video editors almost always come with some sort of catch. The most annoying one is probably a watermark stamped on the export because you often only find out after doing the edit. CapCut used to be the easy answer for quick edits, but more of its basics are now paywalled. Premiere Pro is the opposite of that - it's a fantastic editor but paying Adobe every month to stitch clips together is a waste of subscription.

An open-source editor that runs entirely in a browser tab caught my attention lately, called OpenCut. So I spent a session editing some clips in it. Here's why this editor is worth considering if CapCut has become too restrictive for you or if Premiere is a little overboard…

Can't use CapCut? Here are 8 free video editing apps to use instead

You should always learn a free video-editing tool as backup

1
By  Ruby Helyer

What is OpenCut?

There's a browser version and a GitHub rewrite

OpenCut is a free video editor, and its GitHub page is pretty upfront about its philosophy since it's tagged as the open-source CapCut alternative. Its pitch is a bit of a dig at CapCut paywalling its basic features, though it also emphasizes privacy, with the promise that your content stays on your device. It's sitting at over 80k stars on GitHub at the time of writing, which is quite a lot for a project still in beta.

The fact that it's primarily browser-based is one of the reasons I was drawn to it, so it wasn't yet another bulky piece of software to install. Browsers can do a lot more than in terms of editing tools than they get credit for. OpenCut exports through WebCodecs, the browser's own built-in video encoding, and the April update swapped the old WebGL renderer for a Rust compositor compiled to WebAssembly, so the rendering is fast compiled code running on your GPU.

Browser-based usually means your footage gets uploaded somewhere, but OpenCut never uploads your video or audio, and even auto captions run on-device, with no account involved at all. So their promise on privacy does seem to hold up.

Here's the part where it can get a little confusing though: opencut.app runs the classic version, labeled early beta, and the team says that's the one to reach for today. The GitHub repo is a ground-up rewrite now, with plugins and an MCP server on the roadmap, which you can't use yet. The classic code was archived back in May, and self-hosting it means Bun, Docker, and environment files, which is a lot of setup for an editor you can just open in your browser, to be honest. So I recommend just going to the browser version for now.

This open-source tool combines Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and After Effects - And it replaced all three for me

I didn't expect it to replace my entire Adobe setup

13
By  Nolen Jonker

What editing in OpenCut actually looks like

item.title: Smart thermostats never actually look at your windows
item.itunes:title: Smart thermostats never actually look at your windows
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
You crack the bedroom window on a cold morning, then get pulled into your day. An hour later, it's still open. If your smart thermostat has open window detection, you'd assume it has this covered. It only covers part of that hour.

The feature never looks at the window. It reads its temperature sensor, sees the room cool too fast, and guesses. Most guesses come with a timer, so the heat switches back on while the window is still open. One of us at XDA has observed that energy spikes every time a window stays open. A cheap sensor on the frame knows the truth, but most thermostats never ask for it.

This is the Home Assistant automation I run that my family actually loves

Use automations for things that matter, not because they exist

By  Joe Rice-Jones

Open window detection is a guess

It doesn't watch the window

You'd expect a feature called open window detection to detect a window. But actually, it detects a draft. Tado says its version looks for sudden changes in temperature or humidity. Netatmo's smart radiator valves watch for a drop in temperature. Nothing in either system ever touches the window.

Netatmo is proud of those sensors. Its own guide says the valves measure temperature to within about a tenth of a degree Celsius. That's roughly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit, a change your skin would never notice. It's impressive, and it's still only a reading of the air.

It works like a motion-sensor light. The light never sees you. It notices something warm moving and clicks on. The thermostat notices a sudden chill and switches the heat off.

Spotting the chill is the easy half. Knowing when it ends is where the guess falls apart.

Stand still, and the porch light clicks off

Your thermostat has the same blind spot

For Tado, that 15-minute timer in the screenshot above isn't laziness. It's the only way to guess. The thermostat's only clue is the change itself, and once the room is cold, nothing is changing anymore. A cold, steady room looks exactly like a room with the window shut. It's the porch light again. Stand still under one long enough, and it clicks off with you right there.

A cold, steady room looks exactly like a room with the window shut.

Netatmo's help page is the most candid one I found. Its valves need at least three minutes to spot an open window. The heat then stays off for about half an hour and comes back on, even if the window is still open. After that, detection switches off for another 30 minutes.

Now picture a bedroom window left open for an hour. By Netatmo's rules, the heat is off for roughly the first half. For most of the second half, the radiator heats a room with an open window, and nothing is stopping it. Tado lets you extend its timer, but that just moves the problem.

A sharper guess won't fix any of this. Something has to touch the window. Else, say hello to bigger electricity bills!

Which smart thermostats use window sensors

Ecobee does, and Google leaves it to you

A contact sensor is the thing that touches it. It comes in two small pieces: a magnet on the window and a switch on the frame. When they pull apart, the sensor knows the window is open. When they meet again, it knows the window is shut. There's no guessing in either direction.

Ecobee is the clearest example of a thermostat that uses one. Its Pause When Open feature waits until a window with an Ecobee sensor has been open for five minutes, then pauses the heat. It resumes once the window has been shut for 30 seconds. For that hour-long bedroom window, the heat stays off from minute five until you close it.

Google's Nest thermostats don't come with anything like this. The newest Nest can even remind you to open your windows, though Google's help page doesn't say how it would know you closed them. Google Home's script editor can fill the gap by changing a thermostat's mode when a window sensor opens.

Home Assistant goes the furthest. A community add-on called Better Thermostat lists "let your windows disable your heating" among its features. But think about it: getting the answer right every time has to cost more than a guess. And that "more" is about $8 here.

The porch light still covers the whole yard

A sensor only knows about one door

The guess has one real advantage, and the porch light has it too. One motion sensor covers the whole front yard, and nobody wires a switch into every gate. A guessing thermostat watches every window in the room, with no extra hardware to mount.

A contact sensor only knows about the window it's stuck to. Each sensor in the gallery above watches exactly one window. Three windows means three sensors and three batteries to replace.

Then there's the monthly bill. Ecobee's plan table, in the screenshot above, shows an odd split. The free plan already alerts you when a window opens. Pausing the heat needs the Plus plan, at $5 a month. Your thermostat knows the window is open for free. Doing something about it costs extra. The free market world, as we know.

Bosch's smart radiator thermostats are really smart here. They watch for a falling temperature on their own, and then shut themselves down as soon as a window opens.

item.itunes:summary:
Building a PC from entirely new parts in the current hardware landscape is a tall ask if you're on a budget. RAM is the headline cost, with kits costing double or even triple what they used to for the same capacity, but GPUs have also become incredibly pricey, and it's easy to feel numb to that if you're an enthusiast. GPUs have been selling for well above MSRP far more than they've been selling near those prices, but there's one card in particular that stands out. It, too, sells at above its launch MSRP, but it's impossible to ignore the value proposition.

AMD's Radeon RX 9070 XT is far and away the best bang-for-buck GPU available at the moment if you're buying new and targeting high-resolution, high refresh-rate gaming. Roughly, you'll save around $400 by buying the Radeon card with current pricing, which you can pocket and choose the parts you were going to choose with the 5070 Ti, but if you want to spend that $400 on your build, it can make a massive difference.

That $400 can be the difference between running single-channel or dual-channel DDR5, a bigger SSD, a CPU upgrade, or even a monitor resolution bump. Half the price, but nearly identical performance.

By  Jacob Roach

The software conversation needs to be had

In 2026, you're buying a software suite, not just a graphics card

There's an elephant in the room, and that's the software and driver stack of both cards. Nvidia drivers have certainly had their issues since the launch of Blackwell, but since then, it's largely been smooth sailing for most RTX owners. As someone who daily-drives an RTX 5080, there have been a few hiccups with specific driver versions, but they're remedied relatively quickly, and the day-to-day use of things like the Nvidia App and all the ecutraments of the Green Team software stack is smooth.

Then there's AMD's drivers and software stack, which mostly has feature parity, but is just a bit rougher around the edges, and that can be said for many parts of the experience.

For starters, myself and many other users experience driver timeouts consistently, and the cause is difficult to nail down. It can be a conflicting program, a hardware issue, an issue with the driver itself, and it can differ from person to person, making it hard for AMD themselves to nail it down. Just search "adrenalin" or "drivers" on r/Radeon and you'll see what I mean: hundreds of posts describing various issues that you seldom experience on an Nvidia GPU.

In my experience using Adrenalin, it's been hit-and miss. Features like FreeSync, AFMF (AMD's Smooth Motion equivalent), Radeon Anti-Lag, and others absolutely can work flawlessly, but certain setups and settings combinations seem to cause performance issues in certain games. For example, using FreeSync on my 240Hz display introduced unplayable stuttering to every title I tried it on, and this is enabled by default. Turning it on or off for both of my displays concurrently is the only thing that fixed it, while on my Nvidia card, I can use G-SYNC on one monitor at a time if I like with no performance hit. It's the small things like that which make the Nvidia software suite a lot more tolerable.

Then there's the upscaling conversation, but to AMD's credit, their offering has improved significantly with FSR 4—it's just a question of if your chosen game actually supports it. DLSS 4.5 and its Transformer model is supported across all titles that supported DLSS 4, and you'd be hard pressed to find a modern game that doesn't support DLSS 4. FSR 3 has similar support, but the newer version is a bit more sparse, which is frustrating when its a headline feature of the RX 9000 series.

Radeon is still the best choice for an HTPC GPU, and the reason has nothing to do with performance

Nvidia's Linux support is improving, but it's not good enough for controller-first use cases

By  Ty Sherback

AMD does have its own software benefits for certain operating systems

Linux support is rock solid

Ironically, my experience with my AMD card on Linux has been way more stable than on Windows 11, and that speaks to the work AMD has done in that space. AMD's kernel driver is part of Linux itself and its Vulkan driver ships with Mesa, so there's nothing separate to install or keep in sync after updates. FSR 4 works through Proton, too. Nvidia support here has improved a lot and will continue to, but right now, if you're buying a GPU specifically for Linux, Radeon is the way to go.

My RX 9070 XT was the better GPU, but AMD's track record pushed me back to RTX

If they're willing to lock FSR 4 to the newest cards, that's not good news for the longevity of my GPU

12
By  Ty Sherback

Which GPU should you buy

If you're willing to do some troubleshooting and occasionally chase driver ghosts, the RX 9070 XT is currently the best value GPU on the market, despite the fact that it's well over its MSRP. The RTX 5070 Ti simply can't compete in cost-per-frame, but it is a much easier card to slot-in and get gaming quickly, with most of the headline features probably being supported in your game of choice.

item.title: A 1080p Blu-ray can carry more video data than a 4K stream, and once you see why it's hard to unsee
item.itunes:title: A 1080p Blu-ray can carry more video data than a 4K stream, and once you see why it's hard to unsee
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
At this point, I'm sure we all know that 4K has four times as many pixels as 1080p. That's why we've spent the better part of the last decade treating 4K as an obvious upgrade, whether we're buying a TV, a monitor, a console, or even paying more for a streaming plan that actually supports it. Sure, resolution matters, but when you're streaming 4K content on platforms like Netflix, Prime Video, or Hulu, a lot more happens behind the scenes to get that picture on your screen.

In fact, you might be surprised by how much gets sacrificed along the way just because it needs to be streamed. I was reminded of it recently when I watched the 1080p Blu-ray of Dunkirk on my PS5, even though I'd previously streamed it in 4K on Netflix. Of course, I wasn't expecting the Blu-ray to look sharper, but I was surprised by how clean the picture looked despite the lower resolution. Now, I can't take that "4K" label on streaming platforms at face value anymore.

Netflix looks worse on my PC than on a $30 streaming stick, and it isn't the hardware

Netflix looks worse on my PC than on a $30 streaming stick, and it isn't the hardware

1
By  Jasmine Mannan

It all comes down to bitrate

And Blu-ray has a lot of it to work with, even at 1080p

As much as I love talking about resolution, it only tells you how many pixels make up the image, not how much information is actually being used to represent them. That's what bitrate is all about, and it's just as important, especially when you're comparing a Blu-ray to a stream. Simply put, bitrate is the amount of data used per second of video, measured in Mbps. The higher it is, the more information the encoder has to work with when preserving the original image.

Standard 1080p Blu-rays typically have video bitrates somewhere between 20 and 40Mbps. 4K streams, on the other hand, usually fall somewhere around 15–25Mbps, although the exact bitrate depends on the streaming service, title, and codec. The difference here is that Blu-ray uses that much data for a 1080p image, while a 4K stream usually has a slightly lower budget for four times as many pixels. As a result, Blu-ray can preserve fine details, textures, and film grain without aggressive compression. Sure, the 4K stream has the edge in sharpness, but that higher bitrate at lower resolution gives Blu-ray more room to avoid compression artifacts like macro-blocking in complex scenes.

Streaming services aren't just chasing quality

They also need to make sure you're not constantly buffering

Now, you might be wondering why streaming services don't just crank up the bitrate if it can improve image quality. If they did, you'd be much more likely to run into buffering issues, especially if your internet connection isn't fast enough to keep up with thedata being streamed. Netflix recommends an internet speed of 15Mbps or higher for 4K streaming, which is reasonable given how common faster connections have become in recent years. But if a 4K movie needed 40Mbps to take advantage of a higher bitrate, streaming would be less reliable for anyone on a slower connection.

Platforms also have a massive incentive to make every stream as efficient as possible to keep costs low. When millions of people stream at the same time, even a few extra Mbps per viewer can add up to an enormous amount of data that needs to be delivered. A Blu-ray doesn't have to worry about any of this because all that data is already sitting on the disc. It doesn't rely on your bandwidth or a CDN to deliver the movie, so it has more freedom to prioritize image quality.

4K streaming still has better compression

Newer codecs close the gap, but they can only do so much with a limited bitrate

I know I said earlier that Blu-ray doesn't have aggressive compression, but that doesn't mean it compresses video more efficiently. 1080p Blu-rays still use older codecs such as H.264/AVC, while 4K streaming services use HEVC, and more recently, AV1. Even 4K Blu-rays use HEVC, which is more efficient than H.264 at delivering similar image quality with less data. Efficient codecs allow streaming services to squeeze more out of the limited bitrate they use for 4K, so comparing numbers alone isn't really fair.

Still, a better codec can only do so much when it has less data to work with and far more pixels to account for. When four times as many pixels have to fit within that smaller bitrate budget, efficiency alone often won't be enough to make up the difference. That's why fast-paced scenes, confetti, and other fine textures can be challenging for a 4K stream. Something has to give at that bitrate, and it's usually the finer detail you'd probably never notice unless you were looking for it.

Bitrate matters just as much as resolution, but only sometimes

I'm not saying streaming services should increase the bitrate to make 4K worthwhile because that would take away from the convenience of streaming in the first place. Newer codecs already deliver a sharp 4K image without expecting everybody to have a 100Mbps internet connection. And for most people, the picture quality is more than good enough. But Blu-rays are playing a different game altogether because they're not restricted to a lower bitrate to keep bandwidth requirements in check. The improvements in fine detail may matter to those pixel peepers among you, and once you know what to look for, you won't look at the 4K badge the same way.

It all comes down to bitrate

And Blu-ray has a lot of it to work with, even at 1080p

As much as I love talking about resolution, it only tells you how many pixels make up the image, not how much information is actually being used to represent them. That's what bitrate is all about, and it's just as important, especially when you're comparing a Blu-ray to a stream. Simply put, bitrate is the amount of data used per second of video, measured in Mbps. The higher it is, the more information the encoder has to work with when preserving the original image.

Standard 1080p Blu-rays typically have video bitrates somewhere between 20 and 40Mbps. 4K streams, on the other hand, usually fall somewhere around 15–25Mbps, although the exact bitrate depends on the streaming service, title, and codec. The difference here is that Blu-ray uses that much data for a 1080p image, while a 4K stream usually has a slightly lower budget for four times as many pixels. As a result, Blu-ray can preserve fine details, textures, and film grain without aggressive compression. Sure, the 4K stream has the edge in sharpness, but that higher bitrate at lower resolution gives Blu-ray more room to avoid compression artifacts like macro-blocking in complex scenes.

Streaming services aren't just chasing quality

They also need to make sure you're not constantly buffering

Now, you might be wondering why streaming services don't just crank up the bitrate if it can improve image quality. If they did, you'd be much more likely to run into buffering issues, especially if your internet connection isn't fast enough to keep up with thedata being streamed. Netflix recommends an internet speed of 15Mbps or higher for 4K streaming, which is reasonable given how common faster connections have become in recent years. But if a 4K movie needed 40Mbps to take advantage of a higher bitrate, streaming would be less reliable for anyone on a slower connection.

Platforms also have a massive incentive to make every stream as efficient as possible to keep costs low. When millions of people stream at the same time, even a few extra Mbps per viewer can add up to an enormous amount of data that needs to be delivered. A Blu-ray doesn't have to worry about any of this because all that data is already sitting on the disc. It doesn't rely on your bandwidth or a CDN to deliver the movie, so it has more freedom to prioritize image quality.

4K streaming still has better compression

Newer codecs close the gap, but they can only do so much with a limited bitrate

I know I said earlier that Blu-ray doesn't have aggressive compression, but that doesn't mean it compresses video more efficiently. 1080p Blu-rays still use older codecs such as H.264/AVC, while 4K streaming services use HEVC, and more recently, AV1. Even 4K Blu-rays use HEVC, which is more efficient than H.264 at delivering similar image quality with less data. Efficient codecs allow streaming services to squeeze more out of the limited bitrate they use for 4K, so comparing numbers alone isn't really fair.

Still, a better codec can only do so much when it has less data to work with and far more pixels to account for. When four times as many pixels have to fit within that smaller bitrate budget, efficiency alone often won't be enough to make up the difference. That's why fast-paced scenes, confetti, and other fine textures can be challenging for a 4K stream. Something has to give at that bitrate, and it's usually the finer detail you'd probably never notice unless you were looking for it.

Bitrate matters just as much as resolution, but only sometimes

I'm not saying streaming services should increase the bitrate to make 4K worthwhile because that would take away from the convenience of streaming in the first place. Newer codecs already deliver a sharp 4K image without expecting everybody to have a 100Mbps internet connection. And for most people, the picture quality is more than good enough. item.title: Raspberry Pi's storage bottleneck is worse than you think — here's what I switched to instead
item.itunes:title: Raspberry Pi's storage bottleneck is worse than you think — here's what I switched to instead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For a lot of tech enthusiasts, it's a rite of passage to pick up a Raspberry Pi with grand visions of building a cluster, hosting a home cloud, or running local home automation. It starts out strong, but the moment you try to scale up (like adding multiple Docker containers, compiling heavy Go binaries, and running Plex media transcoding), the Pi hits a brick wall.

Realistically, it might be better for you in the long run to pivot to a modern, energy-efficient x86 and high-end mobile silicon mini PC. For a slightly higher initial investment, you get a complete, robust system with native NVMe speeds, massive RAM headroom, and architectural freedom, while Raspberry Pis remain phenomenal for simple GPIO tinkering and dedicated edge sensors. Using them as primary home servers feels like a compromise.

Upgrading to a budget-friendly or high-performance mini PC unlocks desktop-grade compute, lightning-fast storage, and native x86 virtualization that completely outperforms single-board computers for 24/7 home labs.

5 reasons your Raspberry Pi isn’t as fast as it should be (and how to fix it)

Even a Raspberry Pi needs some fine-tuning to stay in tip-top form

By  Ayush Pande

Raspberry Pi might not always stack up

A mini PC might be a better alternative

Single-board computers can struggle under modern self-hosting workloads compared to active x86/mobile silicon. This is because they have slow I/O bottlenecks, thermal throttling under load, and the hidden Raspberry Pi tax (which means buying official power supplies, Micro HDMI adapters, aluminum armor cases, and high-end A2 microSD cards can be very pricey). This pushes your $35 entry-level board closer to hundreds of dollars when you factor all of these in.

Raspberry Pi's rely on microSD cards or constrained single-lane PCIe/USB bridges for storage. Under heavy database writers like Home Assistant or Immich background indexing, IOPS collapse, leading to card corruption and sluggish response times. The storage that you've potentially spent quite a lot of money on might not even be adequate.

Moving to a mini PC gives you native x86 architecture, so you no longer have to hunt for obscure ARM64 Docker image variants or run into painful compilation errors for specialized self-hosted utilities. You have the advantage of the ecosystem as a whole.

You have to invest in the right machine

There are a wide range of mini PCs on offer

The machine that you pick up will depend entirely on what you're hoping to use it for. There are a range of mini PCs on the market, so I decided to test three versions with very different specifications.

If you're looking for something in the sweet spot of value, the GEEKOM A5 2027 is a great option, featuring an AMD Ryzen 5 7430U CPU. It's the ultimate budget-to-performance bridge as it offers you 6 cores, 12 threads, and an ultra-low 15 W to 25 W idle profile. It handles multi-container Docker stacks, Home Assistant, and light media servers silently, but you might struggle when it comes to local AI.

Another option is the high-end Intel workhorse in the form of the GEEKOM IT13 Max, which features an Intel Core Ultra 9 185H processor. It is built for power users who need heavy multithreading, with 16 cores and 22 threads, dual 2.5 GbE network ports, and robust Wi-Fi 7 for routing and heavy server workflows. It handles intense virtualization, Plex 4K hardware transcoding, and local development environments effortlessly.

And lastly, if you're someone who is looking to push local intelligence right to the edge, then the VZMORE AX9 Max, which features an AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 470 CPU, is one of the best of the best when it comes to specifications. It's powered by Zen 5 architecture and a dedicated NPU pushing up to 55 TOPS. It acts as a powerhouse for running local LLMs like Ollama or LM Studio, and you can also run Frigate compute, vision NVR systems, and heavy-duty agentic workflows right on your local LAN. If you're looking to invest more heavily in local AI, a beast like this will get you there, but it's understandably a lot more expensive.

While a mini PC costs more than a Raspberry Pi, you get so much more out of it that it's a better long-term investment because you don't have to keep upgrading or investing in new tech.

Your Raspberry Pi might still be the right call

A mini PC isn't one size fits all

A mini PC isn't the right call for absolutely everything. Sometimes it is better to keep using your Raspberry Pi. Depending on the job you're hoping to use it for, you might be better off keeping your Raspberry Pi for physical computing projects, GPIO sensor prototyping, LED lighting controllers, or low-power remote network sniffers where physical size and pin headers matter.

Don't get me wrong. I'm not saying you should never purchase a Raspberry Pi anymore. I'm just saying that sometimes a mini PC might be better suited to the job and save you money in the long term.

Using a mini PC for your core home automation server (like Home Assistant), media centers (like Plex or Jellyfin), private photo vaults (like Immich), as well as local AI agents and 24/7 network-attached utility services. These are the places where Raspberry Pi simply can't keep up without you spending an equivalent amount on upgrades for the board.

An easy way to know if you're ready to move beyond single-board computers is by auditing your current Pi bottlenecks. You can do this by checking your CPU load averages and IO wait times in Home Assistant to pinpoint where your Pi is currently choking. Luckily, the transition can be seamless: export your Docker Compose files, spin up Proxmox or clean Linux on your new mini PC, and watch your container deployments snap into place instantly.

item.itunes:title: Your next retro console should actually be a $50 used office PC
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The retro gaming itch has been spreading rapidly worldwide, and manufacturers are launching one console after another to meet demand. From handheld devices to emulation boxes, retro gaming has never been better. You can spend hundreds on a retro console to revisit your favorite NES, SNES, PS2, or GameCube games. But there's a better, cheaper way to do it.

Retro emulation doesn't need much hardware grunt, so even a cheap pre-owned office PC can do the trick. All you need is a 10-year-old desktop or mini PC from eBay, maybe add a small SSD, and install Batocera to get going. You'll be able to play games from nearly every retro console you can think of, all for just $50.

You can buy a dedicated emulation box, but you don't need to

Building your own is actually better

Online marketplaces are full of handheld retro consoles and sticks, depending on the experience you're looking for. From $25 to $250, you can choose based on how recent the console you want to emulate is.
